newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy to break monopoly on newspaper sales.
newsitem.headline: Italy to break monopoly on newspaper sales.

text.p: The Italian government announced plans on Friday to end a retail monopoly on newspapers and periodicals in an attempt to ease a crisis in the publishing industry.
A government statement said the cabinet had approved a draft law, which will now go to parliament, to allow bookshops, tobacconists, bars, petrol stations and supermarkets to sell newspapers.
Sales in Italy at present are restricted to registered newspaper vendors, who usually work from street kiosks known as "edicole".
The statement said expansion of outlets would initially be conducted as an experiment for 18 months with a review by parliament mid-way through and at the end of the exercise.
Daily sales of newspapers have fallen progressively in Italy from 115 copies per 1,000 inhabitants at the start of the 1990s to 105 copies per 1,000 inhabitants in 1995.
Many publishers have taken to selling or giving away inserts with their editions to try to enhance popular appeal.
The inserts can range from tourism guides or small novels to video-cassettes of popular feature films and, in the case of the leftist newspaper l'Unita at one point, extracts from the Bible.
Friday's statement said the liberalisation moves had been conceived in order to defend the existing sales network through kiosks.
But it said a wider network of outlets should help boost sales.

"The measures stem from the conviction that a daily newspaper must go out and look for readers by trying to meet them as far as possible in the course of their daily lives," cabinet undersecretary Arturo Parisi said.
"The existing distribution network manages only in part to meet that requirement," Parisi, who drew up the draft law, said.
The statement said the new outlets would be required to ensure plurality of choice in their selection of newspapers and periodicals on sale and would face fines if they did not.
Media magnate Silvio Berlusconi, who has interests in newspaper and magazine publishing through the Mondadori group and family connections, is leader of Italy's centre-right opposition bloc.
His Fininvest group also owns the Standa chain of supermarkets in Italy.
